interest: Ranges from British wedding greetings in 1941 to Konoe-in-Moscow rumors and a Los Angeles geneticist's claims about the imperial heir.
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.0011) spans October 21, 1941 to November 18, 1942, containing diplomatic communications and public inquiries relating to the Japanese Imperial Family, royal ceremonies, and wartime diplomatic maneuvers. The file begins just weeks prior to the outbreak of the Pacific War with a Tokyo telegram from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reporting King George VI's intention to send wedding greetings to Emperor Hirohito's brother, Prince Mikasa. The middle section comprises correspondence from autumn 1942 initiated by Los Angeles geneticist R. Clay Jackson, who wrote to Mrs. Grew claiming that his proprietary method for prenatal sex control had been adopted by the Japanese court to conceive the Crown Prince, while expressing grievances that Margaret Sanger had received credit and compensation; the State Department politely declined to provide information. The concluding portion contains confidential telegraphic exchanges in November 1942 between Washington, Kuibyshev, and Moscow investigating rumors circulated by French radio in Guadeloupe that Prince Fumimaro Konoe was in Moscow on a special mission, which were debunked by embassy inquiries and by Japanese Ambassador Naotake Sato's repudiation of any 'super ambassadors'.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports that King George VI intends to send wedding greetings to Prince Mikasa and Yuriko Takagi.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that King George VI will send greetings for Prince Mikasa's wedding to Yuriko Takagi.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1665 from Joseph C. Grew (Tokyo) on British Greetings for Prince Mikasa's Wedding

subfiles.about: R. Clay Jackson inquires of Mrs. Grew whether his sex-control theories were applied in the conception of the Japanese Crown Prince.
subfiles.summary: R. Clay Jackson tells Mrs. Grew his sex-determination book led to the Crown Prince's birth and complains Margaret Sanger got the credit.
subfiles.title: Letter from R. Clay Jackson to Mrs. Joseph C. Grew Regarding Sex Control and Imperial Birth

subfiles.about: Printed advertising circulars for R. Clay Jackson's monographs on sex control under the natural solar norm.
subfiles.summary: Promotional circulars for R. Clay Jackson's monographs on the cause and control of sex in human offspring.
subfiles.title: Enclosure: Circulars for 'The Cause and Control of Sex in Human Offspring' by R. Clay Jackson

subfiles.about: The State Department informs R. Clay Jackson that no information is available to answer his questions regarding the Imperial Family.
subfiles.summary: Robert L. Smyth replies for Grew that the Department has no information on R. Clay Jackson's inquiries.
subfiles.title: Letter from Robert L. Smyth to R. Clay Jackson Declining Information on Imperial Inquiries

subfiles.about: Loy Henderson reports from Moscow that rumors of Prince Konoe's or Ambassador Sato's presence cannot be confirmed.
subfiles.summary: Loy W. Henderson reports no confirmation that Prince Konoe was in Moscow; Ambassador Sato had not visited recently.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 462 from Loy W. Henderson (Moscow) on Unconfirmed Rumors of Prince Konoe

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Hull asks Kuibyshev to investigate radio reports that Prince Konoe is in Moscow.
subfiles.summary: Hull asks the Kuibyshev embassy to check a French radio report that Prince Fumimaro Konoe was in Moscow.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 564 from Secretary of State Hull to American Embassy Kuibyshev Regarding Prince Konoe

subfiles.about: Henderson relays reports from Kuibyshev on Ambassador Sato's remarks on the war and denial of 'super ambassadors.'
subfiles.summary: Henderson reports Ambassador Naotake Sato told a neutral diplomat Japan could not stop fighting and there would be no 'super ambassadors' in the Soviet Union.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 472 from Loy W. Henderson (Moscow) on Ambassador Sato and 'Super Ambassadors'
